etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English wilwe, welew, variant of wilghe, from Old English welig, from Proto-West Germanic *wilig, from Proto-Germanic *wiligaz, from Proto-Indo-European *welik- (compare (Arcadian) Ancient Greek ἑλίκη (helíkē), Hittite 𒌑𒂖𒆪 (welku, “grass”)), from *wel- (“twist, turn”).

definitions.definition: Any of various deciduous trees or shrubs in the genus Salix, in the willow family Salicaceae, found primarily on moist soils in cooler zones in the northern hemisphere.

quote.citation: 1912 January, Zane Grey, chapter 8, in Riders of the Purple Sage […], New York, N.Y., London: Harper & Brothers Publishers, →OCLC:
quote.text: […]  and through the middle of this forest, from wall to wall, ran a winding line of brilliant green which marked the course of cottonwoods and willows.

quote.citation: 1917, Edward Thomas, “Adlestrop”, in Poems, London: Selwyn & Blount, page 40:
quote.text: And willows, willow-herb, and grass, / And meadowsweet, and haycocks dry, / No whit less still and lonely fair / Than the high cloudlets in the sky.

quote.citation: 1983 December 3, J. R., “Isak Dinesen, The Life of a Storyteller (review)”, in Gay Community News, volume 11, number 20, page 10:
quote.text: By old age she was emaciated, the bones jutting out of her face and her figure frail as a willow branch.

definitions.definition: A rotating spiked drum used to open and clean cotton heads.
(transitive) To open and cleanse (cotton, flax, wool, etc.) by means of a willow.
(intransitive) To form a shape or move in a way similar to the long, slender branches of a willow.

quote.citation: 1928, Robert Byron, chapter 12, in The Station: Travels to the Holy Mountain of Greece‎[1]:
quote.text: Willowing over the rough cobbles of the little pier stepped a thin, bent figure, adorned with a silver nannygoat’s beard and bobbling eyes interrupted by the rim of a pair of pince-nez.

quote.citation: 1930, Talbot Mundy, chapter 7, in Black Light‎[2]:
quote.text: Joe’s impulse was to sketch her, with her shadow willowing beyond her on the mouse-gray paving-stone; but his left fist, obeying instinct, remained clenched behind his back  […]

quote.citation: 1985, Martin Booth, Hiroshima Joe, New York: Picador, page 394:
quote.text: It was floating a foot under the surface. The eyes were holes. The mouth was a slit cavern of darkness. The hair willowed around the scalp.
The draft-drawn smoke willowed down through the hole and across my face, but I didn’t worry about coughing or sneezing.
